candidates.name: Passengers on the Bus
candidates.description: ACT metaphor: you are the bus driver, unwanted thoughts/feelings are rowdy passengers. You can drive toward your values without obeying them. Core self-as-context intervention.

candidates.name: Quicksand
candidates.description: ACT metaphor: struggling with difficult feelings makes you sink deeper, like struggling in quicksand. Acceptance (spreading out, going still) is counter-intuitive but effective.

candidates.name: Tug of War with a Monster
candidates.description: ACT metaphor: you're in a tug-of-war with a monster (your pain) over a bottomless pit. The solution is not to pull harder but to drop the rope entirely.

candidates.name: Leaves on a Stream
candidates.description: ACT defusion exercise: visualize placing each thought on a leaf and watching it float downstream. Teaches non-attachment to thoughts without suppressing them.

candidates.name: The Chessboard
candidates.description: ACT self-as-context metaphor: you are not the chess pieces (thoughts, feelings) but the board itself. The board holds all pieces without being threatened by any of them.

candidates.name: The Sky and the Weather
candidates.description: ACT self-as-context metaphor: you are the sky, your emotions are the weather. Weather changes constantly but the sky remains. Distinguishes transient experience from stable self.

candidates.name: The Unwelcome Party Guest
candidates.description: ACT acceptance metaphor: difficult emotions are like uninvited guests at your party. Trying to throw them out ruins the party for everyone. Better to let them stay while you host.

candidates.name: The Struggle Switch
candidates.description: ACT metaphor by Russ Harris: imagine a switch at the back of your mind. When ON, you struggle with every uncomfortable feeling, creating suffering on top of pain. Turning it OFF is acceptance.

candidates.name: Clean Pain vs Dirty Pain
candidates.description: ACT distinction: clean pain is the unavoidable suffering of being human. Dirty pain is the suffering we add by struggling with clean pain (anxiety about anxiety, guilt about guilt).

candidates.name: The Mind as a Radio
candidates.description: ACT defusion metaphor: your mind is like a radio that plays negative commentary. You can't turn it off, but you can turn down the volume and stop taking it literally.

candidates.name: The Values Compass
candidates.description: ACT values metaphor: values are like a compass pointing in a direction, not a destination you arrive at. You can always check your heading even when lost.

candidates.name: Dropping the Anchor
candidates.description: ACT grounding technique: in an emotional storm, drop an anchor. It doesn't stop the storm, but it holds you steady so you don't get swept away.

candidates.name: The Choice Point
candidates.description: ACT framework by Russ Harris: at any moment you are at a choice point between moving toward your values or away from them. Internal experiences (thoughts, feelings) show up but don't determine the choice.

candidates.name: The Finger Trap
candidates.description: ACT acceptance metaphor: like a Chinese finger trap, pulling harder (resisting) makes you more stuck. The counter-intuitive solution is to push inward (toward the discomfort).

candidates.name: Ball in a Pool
candidates.description: ACT acceptance metaphor: pushing a beach ball underwater takes constant effort, and it pops back up violently when you let go. Suppressing emotions works the same way.

candidates.name: Demons on the Boat
candidates.description: ACT variant of passengers on the bus: demons (painful emotions) threaten you on your boat, but if you stop fighting them and sail toward your values, they lose their power.

candidates.name: Hands as Thoughts
candidates.description: ACT defusion exercise: hold hands in front of face (fused with thoughts -- can't see). Slowly lower them (defusion). The thoughts are still there but no longer block your view.

candidates.name: Creative Hopelessness
candidates.description: ACT phase where the client recognizes that all their control strategies have failed. Not despair but liberation: if fighting doesn't work, maybe you can try something else entirely.

candidates.name: Externalizing the Problem
candidates.description: Michael White's narrative therapy technique: 'the person is not the problem; the problem is the problem.' Separating identity from problem creates agency to resist it.

candidates.name: Re-Authoring
candidates.description: Narrative therapy: the client is the author of their life story, and dominant problem-saturated narratives can be rewritten by finding and amplifying 'unique outcomes' that contradict the problem story.

candidates.name: Holding Space
candidates.description: Therapeutic stance that has migrated into coaching, management, and UX: creating a container where someone can feel without being fixed. Doing less is doing more.

candidates.name: The Therapeutic Alliance
candidates.description: Bordin's concept: therapist and client form an alliance (military metaphor) with agreed goals, tasks, and emotional bond. Has migrated into UX (user-product alliance) and management.

candidates.name: Rupture and Repair
candidates.description: Safran's concept: breakdowns in the therapeutic relationship are not failures but opportunities. A repaired alliance is stronger than one never ruptured. Has migrated into relationship coaching and team dynamics.

candidates.name: Unconditional Positive Regard
candidates.description: Rogers' concept: accepting the whole person without conditions. The metaphor is acceptance-as-sunlight -- it doesn't discriminate. Migrated into parenting, education, and management philosophy.

candidates.name: Transference
candidates.description: Freud's concept: feelings about past figures are 'transferred' onto the therapist. The spatial metaphor (transfer as movement of feelings from one vessel to another) has become a general term for misplaced emotional reactions.

candidates.name: Window of Tolerance
candidates.description: Dan Siegel's concept: a window (bounded aperture) through which you can process experience. Too much arousal pushes you above (hyperarousal), too little below (hypoarousal). Widely adopted in trauma therapy and education.

candidates.name: Felt Sense
candidates.description: Gendlin's focusing concept: a pre-verbal bodily knowing that is more than emotion and more than thought. The body 'knows' before the mind articulates. Migrated into UX research and design thinking.

candidates.name: The Body Keeps the Score
candidates.description: Van der Kolk's metaphor: trauma is tallied in the body like a ledger. The body is an accounting system that records what the mind tries to forget. Has reshaped trauma treatment.

candidates.name: The Inner Child
candidates.description: The adult self contains a child-self that still carries old wounds and needs. Therapeutic work involves reparenting this inner child. Widely used in self-help, coaching, and pop psychology.

candidates.name: Shadow Work
candidates.description: Jung's concept: the shadow is the disowned part of the self, cast by the light of the persona. Integrating (not eliminating) the shadow is the work. Has migrated into leadership development.

candidates.name: Defense Mechanisms
candidates.description: Freud's military metaphor: the ego deploys defensive fortifications (denial, projection, sublimation) against threatening impulses. The self is a fortress under siege from within.

candidates.name: The Presenting Problem
candidates.description: Clinical term with theatrical metaphor: the problem 'presents' itself on stage, but the real issue is backstage. Distinction between manifest complaint and latent dynamics. Used in consulting and diagnostics.

candidates.name: Pendulation
candidates.description: Somatic Experiencing concept by Peter Levine: therapeutic oscillation between activation (trauma state) and resource (safety). Like a pendulum, the nervous system swings between states and finds equilibrium.

candidates.name: Titration
candidates.description: Somatic Experiencing: approaching trauma in small, measured doses like a chemist adding reagent drop by drop. Too much too fast overwhelms; the right amount allows processing.

candidates.name: Containment
candidates.description: Bion's concept: the therapist acts as a container for the client's unbearable emotions, metabolizing them and returning them in digestible form. Widely used in management (leader-as-container).

candidates.name: Mirroring
candidates.description: Kohut's self psychology: the therapist (or parent) mirrors the client's experience back, providing the reflective surface needed for self-recognition. Migrated into coaching and active listening.

candidates.name: Scaffolding (Therapeutic)
candidates.description: Vygotsky-derived concept applied to therapy: temporary support structures that enable the client to do work they cannot yet do alone. The scaffolding is removed as capacity grows.

candidates.name: Working Through
candidates.description: Freud's Durcharbeitung: psychological change requires repeatedly working through (like kneading dough or working through rock) resistant material. Insight alone is not enough; the labor of repetition is required.

candidates.name: Cognitive Defusion
candidates.description: ACT core process: thoughts are 'fused' like a bomb fused to detonate. Defusion is removing the fuse -- the thought remains but loses its explosive power to control behavior.

candidates.name: Psychological Flexibility
candidates.description: ACT's central construct: the mind can be rigid (brittle, breaking under pressure) or flexible (bending without breaking). The hexaflex model maps six processes that contribute to flexibility.

candidates.name: Unique Outcomes
candidates.description: Narrative therapy (White & Epston): moments when the problem's influence was resisted or absent. These exceptions to the dominant story become seeds for an alternative narrative.

candidates.name: The Absent but Implicit
candidates.description: Narrative therapy (White): when someone expresses pain, there is an implicit value being violated. The therapist names what is absent (the cherished value) to connect pain to meaning.

candidates.name: Double Listening
candidates.description: Narrative therapy: simultaneously listening to the problem story AND the counter-story (values, skills, hopes) embedded within it. Requires hearing what is said AND what is not said.
